notes.meaning: Leaders from all the tribes of Israel gathered at Hebron to make David their king. With Saul and his son Ish-bosheth dead, the people recognized that they shared common family roots with David through their ancestor Jacob. They were eager to unite under his leadership after a painful civil war.

The people remembered how David had faithfully led Israel's troops to victory even during Saul's reign. Most importantly, the Lord had already chosen David to rule, calling him to shepherd His people with loving care. A true ruler is called to protect and provide for his people like a shepherd caring for a flock.

The leaders of Israel met with David to establish a covenant, which is a sacred and binding agreement made before the Lord. David promised to govern justly according to God's law, and the people promised their loyal obedience. Then they anointed him with oil, marking his third anointing as he finally took the throne over the united kingdom.

David stepped onto the throne at thirty years of age, the same age Levites began their temple service and Jesus later began His public ministry. God had trained him through fifteen years of trials and exile to prepare him for this great responsibility. He led the tribe of Judah from Hebron for seven and a half years before ruling the entire nation from Jerusalem for thirty-three years.

David led his soldiers to capture Jerusalem, a Canaanite stronghold sitting high on a steep mountain. The Jebusites felt so safe behind their high walls and deep ravines that they mocked David. They insolently claimed that even injured, blind, or lame people could easily guard the fortress against his army.

Despite the proud mockery of the Jebusites, David and his men conquered the rocky fortress on Mount Zion. This high stronghold became David's personal headquarters. He named it the City of David, and it became the capital of the united nation.

David directed his soldiers to enter the city by climbing up the water shaft or steep drainage passage. Taking up the enemy's insults, he called the defenders 'the blind and the lame' because they had openly mocked him and his God. This event gave rise to a common saying to describe unwelcome people who are shut out from important places.

David made the captured stronghold his personal home and capital. He strengthened the city by building defensive walls and stone terraces, starting from the Millo—a major fortification or town tower—and working inward. This secure wall protected the royal residence and closed any weak gaps along the hillside.

David steadily increased in power, honor, and influence as his kingdom grew strong. His success did not rest on his military brilliance alone, but on the continual favor and presence of the Lord. When God fights for His people, no enemy or obstacle can prevent His plans from succeeding.

Hiram, the ruler of the wealthy coastal city of Tyre, sent ambassadors to establish a peaceful alliance with David. Because Israel lacked experienced builders and craftsmen after years of war, Hiram supplied fine cedar timber and skilled workers to construct David a royal palace. This friendly treaty showed that neighboring nations now respected Israel as a major power.

David recognized that his rise to kingship was God's doing, not his own achievement. He understood that God had blessed his royal rule for the benefit and protection of Israel, not to feed his personal pride. God exalts leaders so that they may serve and bless the people entrusted to them.

Once settled in Jerusalem, David took additional wives and concubines, fathering more children. While kings often did this to build political ties and show royal prestige, it directly violated God's command that Israel's kings must not multiply wives. This compromise sowed seeds of division that brought great pain to his household later in life.

This list records eleven sons born to David after he made Jerusalem his capital city. The first four sons listed were born to Bathsheba, looking ahead to family events that unfolded later in his reign. Among these sons was Solomon, whom God chose to succeed David on the throne and build the temple.

When the Philistines discovered that the divided tribes had united under David, they moved swiftly to crush his kingdom before it grew stronger. Knowing their intentions, David marched down to a fortified stronghold to prepare for battle. The Philistines failed to realize that David carried the Lord's presence with him, which Saul had lost.

The Philistines deployed their large army across the Valley of Rephaim, a fertile plain just southwest of Jerusalem. By camping so close to the city, they intended to cut off David's supplies and capture his new capital. Their vast numbers made an imposing show, but spreading out widely made them an easy target for God's judgment.

Even though David was an experienced warrior with a large army, he refused to take action without seeking God's will. He asked the Lord whether he should attack and whether God would grant him victory. God told him to go forward, promising that the enemy would certainly be handed over to him.

David confronted the Philistine army and won a decisive victory. He compared God's power to a raging flood that breaks through a dam and sweeps away everything in its path. To honor God for the victory, David named the site Baal-perazim, which means 'the master of breakthroughs.'

The Philistines had carried the statues of their false gods into combat, hoping their idols would protect them. When the battle turned against them, they fled in panic and abandoned the useless statues on the field. David and his men gathered these idols and burned them with fire, obeying God's law to rid the land of false worship.

Hoping to recover from their bitter loss, the Philistines gathered a large force and returned to the same valley. They refused to accept that God was fighting against them, and stubborn pride led them back into danger. Their return challenged David's trust in God a second time.

Rather than relying on the battle plan that worked before, David sought fresh guidance from the Lord. God instructed him not to launch a frontal charge, but to march quietly around behind the enemy lines near a grove of trees. This shows that God uses careful planning and human obedience alongside His divine power.

God gave David a miraculous signal: the rustling sound of a marching army stirring in the treetops. That sound was proof that the Lord and His heavenly hosts were moving ahead to strike down the Philistine forces. When believers know God is going before them, they must act with boldness and urgency.

David obeyed God's instructions exactly, moving only when he heard the divine signal. As God had promised, Israel routed the invaders, chasing them about eighteen miles across the hill country back toward their own borders. Complete obedience to God brings complete deliverance from our enemies.
